commentary.bottom_line: Fourteen frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries endorse documenting dataset provenance, metadata, and demographic attributes, and three studies show that missing race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic data prevented subgroup bias analysis. No study has tested whether documentation practices lead health systems or developers to detect or correct bias.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Three hazard studies consistently report that missing demographics limited fairness analysis. These are a descriptive deployment study, a retrospective replay, and an automated benchmark. They show that the problem occurs. They do not show that documentation or case-by-case missing-attribute handling solves it.

In one real deployment with 254 patients, race/ethnicity and socioeconomic status were not collected during routine device use. As a result, no one could check whether the device performed worse for any subgroup. A performance gap that is never measured cannot be caught before it reaches patients. Documentation may make such gaps visible, but that effect has not been tested.

In a Canadian cohort of 319,012 angiography outpatients, ethnicity was unknown for 57%. This suggests that routine data capture does not reliably record these fields. The endorsing guidance proposes datasheets and plain-language dataset factsheets. No supplied study reports the staff time, completeness, or fidelity of such documentation in real workflows.

An automated audit across 7 cohorts could not assess 30% of studies because race was never recorded. Two of the hazard studies focused on racial and ethnic minority populations. None reported Medicaid status, safety-net setting, language preference, or literacy. The attributes most relevant to those groups may therefore be absent even where race is captured.

The endorsements come from an assurance framework, consensus guidance including a multi-society radiology statement, and commentaries, all phrased at the should level. None of the supplied sources is a binding rule. No supplied study examines whether documentation expectations change developer or health-system behavior.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares settings that adopt structured dataset documentation with settings that do not. Such studies should measure demographic field completeness, the share of models that receive subgroup performance audits, and whether those audits detect performance gaps that are then corrected. Studies should also evaluate methods for handling missing attributes, such as record linkage or imputation, and report the workload these methods add for data and registration staff.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two hazard studies focused on racial and ethnic minority groups, but none reported insurance type, safety-net status, language, or literacy. Health systems serving these populations therefore have no evidence on whether documentation captures the attributes needed to assess bias for their patients.
